summary:
Firecal is a web application that combines over two decades of NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire observations into a harmonized burning activity calendar. It helps emergency responders, scientists, and land managers explore historical fire patterns, identify unusual activity, and better understand wildfire risks.

Our solution addresses differences between satellite sensors through a dedicated harmonization method, making long-term fire activity more consistent and comparable. Users can explore interactive calendars, monthly anomalies, historical trends, and detailed harmonization reports for selected regions and date ranges.

Firecal also includes a fire spread prediction feature that estimates potential fire development using wind direction, historical fire spread patterns, and the current fire area. By combining historical satellite observations with predictive analysis, the application aims to provide valuable insights into both past fire activity and possible future developments, supporting better monitoring, emergency preparedness, and response decisions.
details:
Firecal – Project Details

What does the project do and how does it work?

Firecal is a web application designed to help emergency responders, scientists, and land managers understand, monitor, and anticipate fire activity. It combines more than two decades of NASA satellite observations from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 in 2026) into one harmonized historical record, and connects it to NASA FIRMS near-real-time detections so that today's fires can be judged against 25 years of history.

Users select a country or the current map view and a date range to explore historical fire activity, identify seasonal patterns, detect unusual conditions, and see where ongoing fires are most likely heading.

Firecal provides several complementary features:

  • Burning Activity Calendar: An interactive year-by-month calendar of harmonized fire activity (Aqua-equivalent fire cell-days) from 2000 to the present.
  • Anomaly View: A diverging color scale showing how each month's fire activity differs from its long-term average, helping identify unusually active or quiet periods.
  • Raw vs. Harmonized Comparison: A chart comparing original satellite hotspot counts with harmonized activity, showing how new satellites create a false upward trend in raw counts.
  • Harmonization Report: A dedicated page presenting the results before and after harmonization, including the calibration factors for each satellite and fire-radiative-power (FRP) class.
  • Live Fires and Spread Forecast: Fires detected in the last 24 hours (NASA FIRMS near-real-time) with their most likely direction for the next 6, 12 and 24 hours, based on real wind and the fire's observed movement.
  • Shareable Searches: Search parameters are stored in the URL, allowing users to share specific regions, date ranges, and views.
  • Data Export: A CSV of all hotspot detections in a search, and a PNG image of every chart.

Our Harmonization Method

Harmonization is the core scientific contribution of Firecal.

MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection characteristics, and the number of satellites in orbit has grown over time, so raw hotspot counts cannot be directly compared. Summing them creates a false upward trend: in our global data, raw counts jump 5.3 times when VIIRS starts in 2012.

We first aggregate detections into fire cell-days: a 0.02° grid cell with at least one vegetation-fire detection by one satellite on a given day. Static industrial heat sources and other non-vegetation detections are removed. Counting active cells rather than individual detections reduces the effect of the different pixel sizes of MODIS (approximately 1 km) and VIIRS (375 m).

However, the relationship between VIIRS and MODIS detections also depends on fire intensity: small fires are often seen only by VIIRS, so a single constant correction factor underestimates big-fire years. Therefore, we calibrate separate factors for each satellite and fire-radiative-power (FRP) class against MODIS Aqua over their overlapping observation period (2012 to present). Calibration is performed per country, with each country's factors shrunk toward the global value to keep them stable where local observations are limited.

Finally, daily fire activity is calculated as a Poisson maximum-likelihood combination of all satellites operating on that day, expressed as Aqua-equivalent fire cell-days. Adding or losing a satellite changes the measurement noise, not the estimated level of fire activity.

The result is a consistent historical time series in which fire patterns and trends matter more than the sensors used to observe them.

Fire Spread Forecast (live)

Beyond historical analysis, Firecal provides a live forecast that helps users understand where an ongoing fire is most likely to go next.

Firecal regularly ingests NASA FIRMS near-real-time detections and groups nearby detections into individual fires. For every fire seen in the last 24 hours, it combines two inputs:

  • Real wind: The current 10 m wind at the fire location (Open-Meteo), which pushes the fire front downwind.
  • Observed drift: Detections of the same fire are grouped by satellite overpass. A weighted fit through their centroids gives the speed and direction in which the fire has actually been moving, and how fast its footprint is growing.

Wind and drift are combined as vectors into a spread cone for 6, 12 and 24 hours, with an arrow showing the most likely path. When wind and drift agree, the cone narrows. For each fire, the application also shows its current area, maximum FRP, movement, wind, and last detection time.

A prototype land-cover layer assigns an alert level based on what lies in the fire's path (urban area: ALARM, forest: WARNING, shrubland: WATCH, cropland: MONITOR). In this version the land-cover classes are simulated and clearly labeled as such in the application.

The forecast is a heuristic decision-support indicator, not a physical fire-behavior model: it does not yet use terrain or fuel, and its reach is limited to 30 km. It is not a replacement for professional fire behavior models or emergency response assessments.

Validation and Results

We first developed and tested the method on Greece, a region with strong fire seasonality and several major fire years.

A single constant MODIS-to-VIIRS correction factor produced approximately 15% yearly error and underestimated the major fire years 2021 and 2023 by 21–33%. With FRP-stratified calibration fitted on 2012–2020 data only, the 2021 and 2023 fire years were estimated within 0–9%.

We then ran the full pipeline on the whole world, 2000–2026, approximately 600 million detections:

  • MODIS-only and VIIRS-only harmonized series agree within 2.9% per year; each of the 30 most active countries agrees within 10%.
  • The raw jumps at the VIIRS launch in 2012 (5.3 times) and at the NOAA-20 launch in 2018 (1.5 times) disappear in the harmonized series (1.02 and 0.94 times, the same as the MODIS-only series).
  • Out-of-sample test: with calibration fitted on 2012–2018 only and tested on 2019 onwards, the yearly error is 4.5% (2019–2024 within ±4%).

Known limitations: at the end of the MODIS mission the reference itself drifts (Terra's orbit since about 2020), which explains a larger error in 2025–2026; a time-varying calibration is the next improvement. After Aqua ends, new satellites will need chained calibration through VIIRS.

These results show why fire intensity and the characteristics of each satellite must be taken into account when combining long-term fire observations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Firecal is designed for emergency responders, scientists, environmental researchers, and land managers who need reliable information about fire activity.

By combining historical analysis, anomaly detection, and a live spread forecast, the application helps users:

  • Identify months and seasons with historically high fire activity.
  • Recognize unusually active periods compared with long-term averages.
  • Compare current fire activity with 25 years of consistent records.
  • See where an ongoing fire is most likely heading in the next 6 to 24 hours, based on real wind and the fire's observed movement.
  • Support monitoring strategies and emergency preparedness.
  • Download data and charts for additional research, analysis, and briefings.

Our goal is to provide a clear picture of both historical fire activity and the likely short-term development of ongoing fires, helping decision-makers act on reliable information.

Tools and Technologies

Firecal is developed using a modern TypeScript-based technology stack.

  • NASA FIRMS: Source of MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations, both the historical archive and near-real-time data.
  • Open-Meteo: Current wind data for the spread forecast.
  • TypeScript: Main programming language used throughout the project.
  • DuckDB: Processing, harmonization, aggregation, and analytical queries.
  • Parquet: Columnar storage for the global satellite dataset.
  • Node.js and Fastify: Backend API for archive and live data.
  • React and Vite: Frontend application.
  • MapLibre GL: Interactive maps.
  • Apache ECharts: Interactive calendars, charts, and data visualizations.

The architecture separates data processing, backend queries, and frontend visualization. The same pipeline runs for one country or the whole world by changing configuration, not code.

Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation of Firecal is combining two complementary capabilities in one application: a scientifically grounded, harmonized 25-year fire record and a live view of where current fires are heading.

Instead of simply displaying MODIS and VIIRS observations together, we address their measurement differences through spatial aggregation, satellite-specific and FRP-stratified calibration, and statistical combination, and we validate the result on the whole world, including an out-of-sample test.

On top of this harmonized foundation, near-real-time detections are measured against the same history, and each live fire gets a forecast that combines real wind with the fire's own observed movement.

Users can investigate historical trends, examine monthly anomalies, understand the harmonization process, compare raw and corrected observations, and follow live fires and their likely paths in one interface.

Factors Considered During Development

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: Satellite resolution, detection characteristics, fire intensity, and the changing number of operational satellites.
  • Data quality: Filtering out non-vegetation detections, including static industrial heat sources.
  • Historical consistency: Avoiding artificial upward trends caused by the introduction of additional satellites.
  • Validation: Testing the harmonization globally and against later years not used for calibration.
  • Forecast honesty: Combining real wind with observed fire movement, and clearly stating what the forecast does not yet include (terrain, fuel) and which layer is simulated.
  • Performance: Efficient processing and querying of a global dataset without sending raw satellite archives to the browser.
  • Accessibility: Intuitive visualizations and colorblind-friendly color scales.
  • Scalability: The same system supports a single country or the whole world.

Firecal turns complex satellite observations into consistent, accessible, and actionable information, helping communities and emergency responders understand historical fire patterns, recognize unusual activity, and anticipate how current fires may develop.
